snippet.title: Generative AI vs Narrow AI: The Difference Explained! #artificialintelligence #architecture #build
snippet.description:
Not all Artificial Intelligence is the same! 🤯 Did you know there are different types of AI, each with very different capabilities?

In this video, discover the difference between Narrow AI and Generative AI, how they work, and how they are transforming our everyday lives.

🤖 NARROW AI: Powers virtual assistants, facial recognition, and recommendation systems.

🚀 GENERATIVE AI: Creates new content, including text, images, audio, and videos using patterns learned from existing data.

But here's the fascinating part: Generative AI is not necessarily a completely separate category from Narrow AI. And neither automatically possesses human-like consciousness.

From AI-generated architectural designs to intelligent digital assistants, artificial intelligence is changing how we work, create, and build the future.

💬 Which type of AI do you think will have the biggest impact on humanity?

snippet.title: Every Level Of Intelligence Explained in 10 Minutes
snippet.description:
A blob with no brain designed a railway map almost as good as Tokyo's. A crow can remember your face for seventeen years. And a five-year-old chimp beat university students at a memory test. This video climbs every level of intelligence, from a single cell to a brain the size of a planet, and asks each one the same question: can it outsmart you? From the slime mold, the bee, the octopus, the dog, the crow and the chimpanzee, through the baby, you and the genius, to all of us together, artificial intelligence and a planet-sized brain.

Every level comes with the experiment behind it. Comparisons like "three million years of counting", "two hundred thousand years of reading" and "a million of your brains" are our own rounded calculations from the published numbers.

#intelligence #brain #animals

0:00 Intro: can it outsmart you?
0:21 The slime mold (0 neurons)
1:13 The bee
2:02 The octopus
2:54 The dog
3:39 The crow
4:37 The chimpanzee (try the memory test)
5:23 The baby
6:11 You
7:00 The genius
8:00 All of us
8:46 Artificial intelligence
9:40 A brain the size of a planet
10:29 Final score

snippet.title: Why Your Index Fails: The Range Column Trap! 🛑 #sql #database #programming
snippet.description:
Why is your composite index performing a slow partial scan even when both columns are in your WHERE clause?

Look at the exact order of your index keys!

In a B-tree index, as soon as the database engine encounters an inequality or range operator—such as greater than, less than, or BETWEEN—it CANNOT seek any subsequent columns in the index.

If your composite index defines OrderDate first and CustomerID second, the engine seeks the date boundary, but must evaluate CustomerID as a slow residual predicate across thousands of rows!

The fix is an enterprise indexing golden rule: Equality columns ALWAYS go first!
Reorder your composite index keys so equality filters come first:
CREATE INDEX IX_Orders ON dbo.CustomerOrders (CustomerID, OrderDate) INCLUDE (TotalAmount);

Now the engine executes a pure two-column B-tree seek!

snippet.title: Aynı Anda Milyonlarca İşlem: Dağıtık SQL Nedir? 🍔 #shorts
snippet.description:
Dev sistemler aynı anda milyonlarca işlemi, hesaplar hiç şaşmadan nasıl işler?

Çok popüler bir hamburgerci düşünün: kapıda binlerce kişi, ama tek bir kasa (veritabanı).
🍔 Geleneksel SQL: Daha büyük bir kasa alır, ama tek kasanın bir sınırı vardır.
🍔 NoSQL: Her yere kasa açar, her kasa kendi defterini tutar; defterler sonradan eşitlenir, bir an için hesaplar tutmayabilir.
🍔 Dağıtık SQL: Her yere kasa açar ama hepsi aynı deftere yazar. Her sipariş, kasaların çoğunluğu "tamam" demeden kesinleşmez. Bir kasa kapansa bile diğerleri çalışmaya devam eder.

Bedeli: Kasalar birbirine danıştığı için her işlem birkaç milisaniye daha uzun sürer.

Sonuç: SQL'in güvenilirliği + NoSQL'in ölçeği bir arada.
Örnekler: Google Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB

Konunun tamamı (11 veri saklama yöntemi) kanaldaki uzun videoda. Yazılımla ilgilenen arkadaşına göndermeyi unutma!

snippet.title: SQL BOSS #1: ADD_MONTHS and the Last Day of the Month
snippet.description:
Boss puzzle: what do these two ADD_MONTHS calls return?
ADD_MONTHS(DATE '2026-01-31', 1) and ADD_MONTHS(DATE '2026-02-28', 1)
Answer: C. Feb 28 and Mar 31.
If a date is the last day of its month, Oracle returns the last day of the resulting month. So Feb 28 plus one month is Mar 31, not Mar 28. Jan 31 plus one month is Feb 28, because February is shorter.
Full explanation of dates in Oracle: see the related video (Oracle Dates in PL/SQL).

snippet.title: How many rows does a CROSS JOIN return in SQL? | Ep 27 #shorts
snippet.description:
Three sizes and two colours give six rows, not three.

How many rows does this return?

SELECT size, colour
FROM sizes
CROSS JOIN colours;

How SQL runs it, step by step:
1. FROM sizes: FROM sizes starts with the sizes table, as always.
2. CROSS JOIN colours: CROSS JOIN colours brings in the second table, with its two rows.
3. SELECT size, colour: SELECT size, colour keeps those two columns.

Takeaway: Every pair, on purpose. Write CROSS JOIN, then count: 3 x 2 = 6.

snippet.title: How do you do a self join in SQL? | Ep 26 #shorts
snippet.description:
This self join looks right. Is the boss in the result?

SELECT e.emp_id, e.name,
  m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN employees m
ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;

The fix:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;

How SQL runs it, step by step:
1. FROM employees e: FROM employees e gives the table the alias e, the employee side of the join.
2. INNER JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id: Then INNER JOIN pairs each e row with the m row whose emp_id matches its manager_id.
3. SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, m.name AS manager: Last, SELECT keeps the employee's name, and the boss's name as manager.
Fix: LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id: The fix is LEFT JOIN.

Takeaway: Join a table to itself. LEFT JOIN keeps the boss. Use LEFT JOIN when a match may be missing.

Follow @visual.sql101 for a new visual SQL lesson every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

snippet.title: Se registró con el nombre “admin” aunque ya existía y accedió al panel de administración 👤🔓
snippet.description:
Detrás de una web suele haber una base de datos que guarda los usuarios y sus contraseñas. El usuario con más privilegios es el administrador, cuyo nombre es “admin”: para el sitio, si tu cuenta se llama así, tienes todos los permisos. Y como ya existe, nadie más debería poder registrarse con ese nombre.

Pero hay dos detalles. En la tabla, el nombre de usuario tiene un límite de 20 caracteres y, si pasa, se recorta lo que sobra. Y al comparar dos nombres, los espacios del final no cuentan. Un hacker lo aprovecha: se registra como “admin”, muchos espacios y una letra al final. El servidor busca ese nombre completo, no existe, y lo acepta. Pero al guardarlo, la base de datos lo recorta y queda solo “admin”. Ahora hay dos cuentas admin: la original y la del hacker, que entra con su propia contraseña y abre el panel de administración.

Esto se llama SQL truncation.

Parte 28 de la serie sobre vulnerabilidades web.

#sqltruncation #ciberseguridad #hacking #seguridadweb #websecurity #cybersecurity #basesdedatos #pentesting #shorts

snippet.title: What is SQL? An Excel sheet stops at 1,048,576 rows. How do apps find your orders? SELECT FROM WHERE
snippet.description:
What is SQL? An Excel sheet stops at 1,048,576 rows. The apps you use every day hold far more than that, and still find your row in a blink. Here's how 👇

A spreadsheet works until it doesn't: a sheet can't hold more than 1,048,576 rows. Apps keep their data in databases instead, and ask for it in SQL.

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language for asking a database for data.

Think of it like a library:
📚 The database = the library
🗂️ A table = one shelf of cards, every card filled in the same way
🙋 A SQL query = asking the librarian "every book Ana borrowed, please": you say what, the librarian knows where

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀:
→ A database stores data in tables: rows (one per order) and columns (buyer, item)
→ You write a query: SELECT item FROM orders WHERE buyer = 'Ana';
→ SELECT picks the columns, FROM the table, WHERE the rows
→ The query never says how to search: the database works out how to find the rows, and sends back only those

A few things that surprise people:
→ SQL became an official standard in 1986, and it's still revised (the latest version is SQL:2023)
→ Postgres, MySQL and SQLite each differ a little, but SELECT, FROM and WHERE work the same in all three
→ Without ORDER BY, a database doesn't promise any order for the rows it returns
→ In Stack Overflow's 2026 survey, 58.4% of respondents used SQL, second only to JavaScript, and PostgreSQL was the most used database

SQL gets mixed up with the databases themselves: SQL is the language; PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite are databases that understand it.

The app doesn't hunt for your rows: it describes them in SQL, and the database works out how to find them.

Save this for the first time someone asks you what SQL actually is.

🦆 Next in the course: SQL joins, on the same people and their orders.

Before the end, what did you guess: do apps search for your row, or ask for it? 👇

snippet.title: Stop writing UNION in SQL when you really need UNION ALL! ⚠️
snippet.description:
Stop writing UNION in SQL when you really need UNION ALL! ⚠️

Combining datasets from multiple queries is fundamental, but writing UNION by default is a major performance killer.

❌ The UNION Trap:
SELECT user_id, amount FROM q1_sales
UNION
SELECT user_id, amount FROM q2_sales;
- UNION forces an implicit SORT and DISTINCT deduplication pass across the entire result set.
- On large tables, this exhausts memory buffers and spills to disk, causing massive query slowdowns!

✅ The Senior Solution (UNION ALL):
SELECT user_id, amount FROM q1_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT user_id, amount FROM q2_sales;
- UNION ALL performs zero sorting and simply streams the row batches together.
- Up to 10x faster execution and drastically lower cloud warehouse compute cost!

The Golden Rule:
Always default to UNION ALL. Only switch to UNION if you explicitly need duplicate removal.

snippet.title: Как работает JOIN в SQL: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS и SELF наглядно
snippet.description:
SQL JOIN соединяет данные из таблиц. Но какие строки попадут в результат, где появятся NULL и почему одна запись может превратиться в несколько?

Разбираем соединения на примере команд и пилотов:
• JOIN и INNER JOIN - пары, подходящие под условие ON
• LEFT, RIGHT и FULL OUTER JOIN - сохранение строк без совпадений
• CROSS JOIN - все возможные комбинации
• SELF JOIN - соединение таблицы с самой собой

snippet.title: This SQL Query Returns ZERO Rows. Why? (NOT IN + NULL)
snippet.description:
This query returns zero rows, and nobody can see why.

We want every customer who has never placed an order:
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);

But one row in orders has a NULL customer_id.

Why it breaks:
• NOT IN means "not equal to EVERY value in the list"
• Comparing anything to NULL gives UNKNOWN, not TRUE
• One UNKNOWN in that chain, and no row can ever pass the filter

✅ The fix: NOT EXISTS, which handles NULLs the way you expect.

💾 Save this one. It's a classic interview question.
